title: Split finishers into four pace groups
prompt:
A trail race stores every registered runner with their finish time in seconds. Runners who did not finish have a NULL finish time.

The organisers want to split the finishers into 4 pace groups for next year's start waves: group 1 is the fastest, group 4 the slowest.

- Columns: bib, finish_seconds, pace_group
- Only runners with a finish time; NULL finishers get no row
- Order runners by finish_seconds ascending; equal times are ordered by bib ascending
- Groups are as even as possible; when they can't be equal, the faster groups get one extra runner each (10 finishers → 3, 3, 2, 2)
- With fewer than 4 finishers, each runner gets their own group starting at 1
- Any row order is fine
hints: Postgres has a window function that deals rows into a fixed number of buckets.
ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY ...) already gives earlier buckets the extra rows. Make sure the order is total.
Filter WHERE finish_seconds IS NOT NULL before the window runs, and use ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY finish_seconds, bib).

exercise.schema: CREATE TABLE runners (bib int PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL, finish_seconds int);
exercise.starter:
-- Pace groups
SELECT bib, finish_seconds,
       ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY finish_seconds) AS pace_group
FROM runners;
exercise.solution:
SELECT bib, finish_seconds,
       ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY finish_seconds, bib) AS pace_group
FROM runners
WHERE finish_seconds IS NOT NULL;

tests.name: ten finishers split 3-3-2-2
tests.seed: INSERT INTO runners SELECT g, 'Runner ' || g, 3700 - 60 * g FROM generate_series(1, 10) g;

hiddenTests.name: five finishers split 2-1-1-1
hiddenTests.seed: INSERT INTO runners SELECT g, 'Runner ' || g, 100 * g FROM generate_series(1, 5) g;

hiddenTests.name: nobody finished
hiddenTests.seed: INSERT INTO runners VALUES (1, 'Hal', NULL), (2, 'Ivy', NULL);

explanation: ntile(4) deals the ordered rows into 4 buckets whose sizes differ by at most one, and the larger buckets come first, which is exactly the rule in the prompt. The WHERE clause runs before window functions, so filtering out NULL finish times makes the buckets cover finishers only. Without the filter, NULLs sort last in ascending order and still take up slots, shifting everyone's group. ORDER BY finish_seconds alone is not a total order, so tied runners could land in different groups from run to run; adding bib makes it deterministic.
notes: This is one sort plus a WindowAgg; ntile needs the partition row count, so Postgres buffers the partition before emitting rows. For large tables an index on (finish_seconds, bib) with a partial predicate WHERE finish_seconds IS NOT NULL can supply the order. If you need equal times to always share a group, use a value-based rule such as width_bucket or percent_rank instead of ntile.
followUps: How would you guarantee that runners with the same time always land in the same group?
Return each group's fastest and slowest time instead of one row per runner.
